text: You already write T-SQL. Most company data lives in relational databases, so the smoothest way to start an analysis is to query the database directly from Python and receive the result as a DataFrame — no CSV export, no stale copy sitting around. This lesson shows the pattern, how to pass parameters safely, and how to decide whether to do the work in SQL or in pandas.

To practice without needing a real server, use SQLite, which is built right into Python. Load two small illustrative tables, orders and customers, into an in-memory database with to underscore sql. Then pd dot read underscore sql underscore query takes a plain SQL string and that connection, and hands you back a DataFrame with sensible types already assigned — int64, float64, object.

For SQL Server, the usual approach is a SQLAlchemy engine using the pyodbc driver. Build an engine with your server, database, username, password, and the ODBC driver name, then run read underscore sql underscore query exactly the same way against that engine instead of a sqlite connection. Check your current documentation for the exact driver name — 17 and 18 are both common — and the authentication method you need. And never type a real password straight into a notebook you plan to share; read it from an environment variable instead.

Once connected, you can run any SQL you already know how to write. Join orders to customers, group by city, count orders, and sum the amount, ordering by revenue descending — the database does every bit of that heavy lifting, and Python just receives the finished result as a DataFrame. Nothing in that query is new SQL at all — only the connection line changed.

If a value comes from Python, pass it through params — never paste it directly into the SQL string. Filter for status equals shipped and amount greater than 50 using question-mark placeholders, passing shipped and 50 as a params tuple. Here's why that matters: build the same query with an f-string instead, and feed it a malicious value like shipped-quote-or-one-equals-one, and you get back all six rows — the entire table. Run the parameterized version with that same malicious text, and you get back zero rows, because it's treated as data, not code. Parameters avoid SQL injection entirely.

To underscore sql writes a DataFrame back into the database. Read your city summary query into a DataFrame, then write it into a new city underscore summary table with if underscore exists equals replace. If underscore exists can be fail, the default, replace, or append — choose deliberately, since replace drops the existing table first before writing the new one.

So where should the work actually happen? Filter and aggregate in SQL whenever you can — the database is optimized for exactly that, and it sends you far fewer rows over the wire. Pull the result once, then explore, model, plot, and reshape in pandas, where that's genuinely easier. And mind the dialect — T-SQL's TOP 10 becomes LIMIT 10 in SQLite, so always write SQL in your target database's own dialect.

To recap: read underscore sql underscore query with a SQL string and a connection returns a DataFrame; use a SQLAlchemy engine for SQL Server. Use params, never string-pasting, to pass values safely. To underscore sql with if underscore exists writes results back. And push filtering and aggregation into SQL, pulling only the result into pandas. Next: pulling data from APIs.
